splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's or an agency's anti-defendant interpretation of an ambiguous criminal provision, or instead apply the rule of lenity in the defendant's favor. This affects sentencing enhancements and criminal liability nationwide.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference applies even in criminal or quasi-criminal contexts, and that lenity does not override an agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt in the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or an impermissible expansion of the guideline text. This affects career-offender designations and substantially longer sentences for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a permissible interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as career-offender predicates.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot add what the guideline text omits, so conspiracy does not qualify as a career-offender predicate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenses and creates geographic disparities in sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines even if the substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the underlying substance be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This affects base offense levels and career-offender status for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses without requiring the substance to be federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Henderson as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive sentencing changes—alone or combined with other factors—when evaluating motions for compassionate release. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to permit this, but some circuits hold the Commission exceeded its authority. This affects thousands of prisoners serving sentences that would be substantially lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Commission's policy statement purporting to allow this exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement amendment at § 1B1.13(b)(6).

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced as opposing view in Black

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging BOP decisions about the terms or conditions of confinement (such as denial of First Step Act earned time credits for prerelease custody) must proceed via habeas corpus or may use a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens or the APA).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for challenges to the conditions or execution of a federal sentence, or whether civil rights actions are also available. This matters because habeas requires exhaustion of administrative remedies and has other procedural requirements that differ from civil actions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-of-confinement claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge effectively seeks a speedier release from confinement, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy, and civil rights actions are not available.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP execution-of-sentence decisions may proceed as civil rights actions, not only through habeas corpus.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Fortner as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in a debtor's property between the petition date and the conversion date inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This directly impacts debtors who convert cases in good faith and the recovery available to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity are part of the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of § 541(a) and the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's structure, purpose, and legislative history of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Castleman dissent as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from the denial of a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding and subject to the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Onamuti as minority view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to promoting reentry and public safety.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. Some circuits allow courts to punish the defendant for the violation itself, while others hold that revocation sentences must focus on the breach of trust and the defendant's reentry needs. This creates disparate sentencing outcomes for supervised release violations.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, permitting revocation sentences that serve a punitive purpose.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should not be punitive
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to sanction the breach of trust and address reentry needs, not to punish the underlying violation, placing the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of the split.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Esteras dissent as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA permits plan actuaries to adopt actuarial assumptions after the measurement date when calculating an employer's withdrawal liability. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumptions directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date and cannot be selected or changed after that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the measurement date, so long as the assumptions are applied to data as of that date, giving the actuary flexibility in timing.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced as opposing view in cert petition

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervisory period beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing outcomes at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, so the clock does not run while the person absconds, allowing courts to later revoke supervised release.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for judicially-created fugitive tolling of supervised release, so the term runs even while the supervisee absconds.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Rico v. United States (cert grant context)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits split 6-to-3 on whether the categorical bar in § 2244(b)(1)—prohibiting successive habeas petitions that raise previously presented claims—applies to federal prisoners proceeding under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than § 2255(h) alone would impose, categorically barring any claim previously raised regardless of new evidence or new constitutional law.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates possess Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election administration rules such as ballot-receipt deadlines. The resolution affects the ability to challenge voting procedures nationwide before elections take place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have a cognizable competitive injury sufficient to confer Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute their votes or alter the competitive landscape before an election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections (cert context)

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge ballot-counting rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in cert grant description as opposing view

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the denial of a motion to seal court records containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining medical privacy is a value of sufficiently 'high order' to warrant immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, noting the strong interest in keeping medical treatments and diagnoses private. Other circuits have addressed the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing motions with varying results, creating potential divergence on when privacy-based sealing denials are immediately appealable.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements and must await final judgment for appellate review.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in business operations including hospitality, retail, and other service industries. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach to these legal questions, indicating a circuit split of sufficient importance.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applies the Second Circuit's particular legal framework for evaluating discrimination and unfair treatment claims against business operators.

positions.label: Differing approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different legal standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
